title: Closest Pair of Points
description: Find the two nearest points among many, faster than checking every pair

blocks.text: The closest pair problem asks: among a set of points, which two are nearest to each other? It is a classic showcase of how a clever divide and conquer idea beats the obvious approach.
The naive method checks every pair, but we can do far better and reach O(n log n).
You are given n points on the plane and must find the smallest distance between any two of them, and often the pair itself.
It appears in clustering, collision detection, and map applications, anywhere you care about the nearest neighbours in a set of locations.
The straightforward approach compares every pair of points and keeps the smallest distance. Remember to compare squared distances to avoid the slow and imprecise square root.
This is O(n squared), fine for a few thousand points but too slow for large inputs.
We can do much better by splitting the problem. Sort the points by x, then split them into a left half and a right half at the middle. Solve each half recursively.

blocks.caption: Split by the middle x, solve each half, and take the smaller distance d

blocks.text: Let d be the smaller of the two halves best distances. The closest pair is either fully inside one half, already found, or it straddles the dividing line, which we still need to check.
The straddling case looks like it could be expensive, but a neat fact tames it. Any crossing pair closer than d must lie within a thin strip of width d around the dividing line.

blocks.caption: Only points within d of the divide can matter, and each checks just a few neighbors

blocks.text: Sort the strip points by y. Then each point only needs to be compared with a small constant number of the points just ahead of it, because more than that cannot fit within distance d. That is what keeps the merge step linear.

Why only a few neighbors:

Within the strip, points closer than d cannot be packed tightly. Geometry guarantees each point has at most a handful of candidates ahead of it in y order, so the strip scan stays fast.
The recurrence splits the work in half and does linear work to merge, exactly like merge sort. That gives O(n log n) overall, a huge improvement over the quadratic baseline.
For many practical inputs a plane sweep with a balanced set achieves the same O(n log n), and some contexts simply use the brute force when n is small.

items: Clustering points that lie near each other
Collision detection between many moving objects
Map and location services finding the nearest place
Any problem needing the minimum gap in a set of positions

blocks.text: It is also a classic lesson in algorithm design: a smart divide and conquer turning a quadratic problem into a near linear one.
